sourceEvidence.label: RIVT recovery closure repository evidence
sourceEvidence.driftDescription: Packet 90 implements the selected provider-neutral local foundation after the evidence collection was hashed. The collection digest still binds the pre-analysis snapshot; the implementation handoff records the exact source comparison and new local verification boundary.

assessment.summary: RIVT needs one coordinated database-and-object recovery boundary; the fresh logical artifact restores PostgreSQL metadata but not file bytes.

nonNegotiables: No potentially chargeable provider action without Michael's explicit approval immediately beforehand.
No production file contents, object keys, account identifiers, credentials, or database URLs in repository evidence or operator logs.
No production database writes, public restore endpoints, plan upgrades, PITR, or recurring features in the one-time proving drill.
Recovery evidence must distinguish primary availability, one-time copy recovery, and durable independent backup.
assumptions: The approved targets remain a 24-hour RPO, 4-hour RTO, 30-day retention, and 30-day restore-drill cadence.
The read-only 89-object, 40,385,105-byte inventory is a point-in-time observation and can change.
No measured production backup-runner CPU or memory budget was supplied.
Malware scanning, legal retention approval, and provider-contract approval remain separate work.

opportunities.title: Establish a complete database-and-object recovery boundary
opportunities.summary: Bind a consistent encrypted database snapshot and every referenced object to one independently retained recovery point.
opportunities.diagnosis: The logical artifact can rebuild PostgreSQL rows, keys, hashes, and sequences, but object bytes and the database artifact share the production Railway administrative failure domain.

evidence.claim: The fresh artifact records 109 tables and 8,760 rows but has not been restored and does not contain object bytes.
The backup creator serializes public PostgreSQL table rows and sequences, then uploads the encrypted envelope; it does not read referenced file objects.
The restorer requires an isolation attestation, can compare source and target identity, migrates a fresh target, restores transactionally, restores sequences, and enforces strict table-count parity.
Current media classes retain object keys, byte counts, MIME types, and generally SHA-256 values that can support cryptographic recovery verification.
A read-only aggregate check observed 89 objects totaling 40,385,105 bytes across the production buckets without reading keys or contents.
Railway buckets currently do not support object versioning, Object Lock, lifecycle configuration, or native bucket snapshots/backups.
Reading and hashing a current primary-bucket object proves present availability rather than recovery after loss.
A second bucket in the same Railway workspace can prove a one-time copy/restore but remains exposed to the same administrative compromise.

desiredInvariants: Every accepted backup has one immutable snapshot ID binding the encrypted database artifact, source revision, complete object manifest, counts, bytes, and completion state.
Every active referenced object is backed up and cryptographically verified; samples are never represented as full-corpus coverage.
Production backup credentials can append new snapshots but cannot read, overwrite, shorten retention, or delete historical backups.
Recovery credentials are separate from production credentials and are not stored in normal application configuration.
A production Railway account compromise cannot erase retained backups.
Restore targets are provably distinct, empty, private, disposable, and deleted by exact provider identifiers.
Evidence output contains no sensitive identifiers, credentials, URLs, filenames, keys, or customer content.

options.title: Restore-only baseline
options.summary: Restore the exact database artifact and hash objects read from the production bucket.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: It satisfies a database restore drill but leaves the complete object-recovery contract open.
It can prove the exact fresh artifact is restorable.
Primary-bucket reads do not create an independent object recovery source.
The design remains entirely inside the existing Railway boundary.

tradeoffs.assessment: It proves database decryption and replay, but object deletion and production-account compromise remain unrecoverable.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Restore the exact artifact to a distinct empty target and verify strict schema, sequence, count, and future content-digest parity.

tradeoffs.assessment: There is no normal request-path change; a drill temporarily consumes backup-runner and target resources.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure public health, restore duration, CPU, and object-read throughput during a time-boxed drill.

tradeoffs.assessment: Database inserts are batched; any object checker must stream rather than buffer full files or the corpus.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Record peak RSS during the largest qualifying object and full database replay.

tradeoffs.assessment: A database-only recovery path becomes current, while object recovery remains a single-point failure.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject database replay failure and prove transaction rollback and exact temporary-resource cleanup.

tradeoffs.assessment: It reuses prior runbooks but still requires manual temporary service lifecycle and careful secret handling.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run a two-operator checklist review and verify that captured evidence contains no secrets or customer identifiers.

tradeoffs.assessment: The existing application and stored data format remain unchanged.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Run all existing backup utility tests and repository gates without schema changes.

residualRisks: No object can be recovered if it is missing from the primary bucket.
Equal table counts do not prove equal field values.
The current backup creator does not use one repeatable-read database transaction.
The fresh artifact does not cryptographically bind its externally observed source commit.

workPackages: Add exact source/target identity and empty-target preflight.
Run the exact named-artifact restore under a cost authorization.
acceptanceCriteria: The exact fresh artifact restores 109 tables and 8,760 rows with zero count differences and zero pending migrations.
The temporary service and volume are absent after cleanup.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Interrupt the drill and delete only the exact temporary service and volume identifiers; production receives no write.

options.title: Full-corpus Railway snapshot
options.summary: Copy every qualifying referenced object to a blank second Railway bucket and restore from that copy.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: It demonstrates one complete database-and-object recovery cycle but not durable recurrence.
It restores the exact database artifact and binds recovered objects to its metadata.
A complete copy and restore from the second bucket is honest one-time object-byte recovery evidence.
Both copies remain deletable under one Railway administrative boundary.

tradeoffs.assessment: A complete second copy closes one-time recovery proof but does not contain a compromised Railway workspace.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Copy every qualifying object, restore representative classes only from the second bucket, and verify full manifest parity.

tradeoffs.assessment: The drill adds full-corpus reads, writes, hashing, and database restore load outside the request path.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure bytes per second, duration, CPU, public health, and abort if the corpus exceeds the recorded bound plus 10 percent.

tradeoffs.assessment: A streaming design needs bounded hash/encryption buffers rather than corpus-sized memory.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Assert a fixed stream buffer and measure peak RSS against the largest object.

tradeoffs.assessment: The copy proves recovery from source-object loss after snapshot creation, but a common provider/account failure remains.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject missing objects, mismatches, partial writes, retry exhaustion, and teardown failure.

tradeoffs.assessment: Operators must inventory, cap, create, verify, empty, and delete a database service, volume, and bucket by exact ID.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Use before/after provider inventories and fail the drill until every temporary identifier is absent.

tradeoffs.assessment: The repository needs a manifest, bounded copier, privacy-safe logging, storage-scope coverage, and local S3 tests.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Test every storage scope against disposable local PostgreSQL and mocked S3 before any deployment.

residualRisks: The same Railway account can delete or alter both buckets.
Railway buckets do not provide versioning or Object Lock.
One successful copy does not establish daily recurrence or 30-day retention.
Legacy objects without reliable hashes cannot be represented as fully verified.

affectedComponents: new object manifest and recovery verifier
workPackages: Build and locally test complete object inventory and bounded streaming copy.
Add privacy-safe manifest and recovery evidence.
Run one owner-approved capped full-corpus proving drill.
Delete and verify all temporary resources.
acceptanceCriteria: Every qualifying object referenced by the restored snapshot is copied and hash/size verified.
Available album photo, attachment, logo, and evidence classes restore from the temporary copy and pass hash and format checks.
No sensitive identifiers or content appear in evidence.
All temporary resources are removed by exact ID.
migrationNotes: Use this option as a proving stage for the separate immutable destination rather than the final architecture.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Empty the temporary bucket, delete it, then delete the exact temporary PostgreSQL service and volume; stop if any deletion cannot be verified.

options.title: Cross-provider immutable backup
options.summary: Write coordinated client-side-encrypted database and object snapshots to a separately administered provider with versioning and enforced retention.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Scheduled coordinated snapshots plus drills can satisfy the complete recovery contract.
The existing named-artifact path becomes one component of an independently retained recovery point.
File bytes are retained and restored independently of the primary bucket.
The final backup no longer depends on unsupported Railway versioning or immutability.
Versioning and compliance retention protect retained versions, while credentials, key custody, and complete manifests still need direct controls.

tradeoffs.assessment: Separate administration, append-only production authority, client-side encryption, versioning, and immutable retention contain production-account deletion and overwrite paths.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Attempt deletion/overwrite with production credentials, verify denial, then restore with the separately held recovery identity.

tradeoffs.assessment: Scheduled full or incremental snapshots add hashing, encryption, serialization, and cross-provider transfer outside request handling.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure backup duration, CPU, bytes transferred, and public health at current and projected 10x corpus sizes.

tradeoffs.assessment: Streaming keeps buffers bounded, while the manifest index grows with object count and must avoid whole-corpus body retention.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Record peak RSS and manifest memory at current, 10x, and 100x synthetic inventories.

tradeoffs.assessment: A separate provider removes the primary common-mode failure but introduces network, provider, scheduler, alert, and encryption-key dependencies.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Inject destination outage, partial upload, key failure, retry exhaustion, missed schedule, and recovery-credential loss scenarios.

tradeoffs.assessment: RIVT must own a second provider account, least-privilege identities, key escrow, monitoring, retention, legal review, cost review, and recurring drills.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Complete a two-person runbook review, account recovery exercise, alert-delivery test, and provider evidence register.

tradeoffs.assessment: The design requires consistent database snapshots, coordinated manifests, an immutable destination, credential separation, scheduling, and deletion-policy reconciliation.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Roll out through local harness, same-provider proving drill, governance-retention trial, then compliance retention after policy approval.

residualRisks: Loss or compromise of the client-side encryption key.
A systematic backup-runner omission that creates apparently successful incomplete snapshots.
Retention rules that conflict with legal hold, DSAR deletion, or approved purge policy.
Faithful preservation of malware until separate scanning/quarantine is implemented.
Provider and network outage during the RPO window.
Restore tooling drift after schema migrations.

affectedComponents: new coordinated object backup and recovery tooling
workPackages: Build and locally validate the bounded verifier.
Run the owner-approved same-provider proving drill.
Configure a separate provider/account with client-side encryption, versioning, and short governance retention.
Add repeatable-read snapshots, shared snapshot IDs, content digests, and complete manifests.
Split append-only backup and offline recovery credentials.
Enable approved immutable retention and daily scheduling.
Run and time a full isolated restore from the immutable destination.
acceptanceCriteria: Production credentials cannot read, overwrite, shorten retention, or delete accepted backup snapshots.
A daily complete backup stays inside the 24-hour RPO and alerts fail closed.
A monthly isolated database-and-object restore stays inside the 4-hour RTO.
Every referenced object is accounted for, and missing or mismatched bytes fail the snapshot.
Provider, region, retention, key custody, cost, and legal terms are approved and recorded.
migrationNotes: Start with reversible governance retention; enable compliance retention only after deletion and legal-hold policy approval.
Existing retained versions cannot be removed early after compliance retention is enabled.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Before immutable retention, disable writes and delete the trial destination. After compliance retention, disable future writes and allow retained versions to expire according to the approved policy.

opportunities.recommendation: Use a cross-provider immutable backup as the launch target, with a locally reviewed harness and one capped same-provider full-corpus drill as the proving stage.

selectionRecord.authorizedScope: Provider-neutral local foundation and no-cost activation decision only.

openQuestions: Does Michael approve AWS S3 Object Lock, a named separately administered account, a US region, its DPA/subprocessors, and incident route?
Which proposed primary-retention, verified-erasure, legal-hold, and at-least-30-day immutable-object-set rules receive owner and counsel approval?
Which reviewed cryptographic 2-of-3 threshold-key scheme is approved, who are its three custodians, and how is reconstruction tested?
What maximum incremental cost, source bytes, requests, egress, orphan bytes, and expiration are approved for synthetic provider conformance?
Does Michael authorize up to US$1.00 of incremental Railway usage and the exact production-read byte boundary for one physical proving drill?
What recurring monthly ceiling and forecast-alert thresholds are approved?
How should legacy objects without trustworthy SHA-256 values be backfilled or classified while every canonical stored byte remains recoverable?
Which private or CA-verified PostgreSQL path is approved for every backup and restore?
